In itself, however, there lies in this sensing and imagining behavior of intuition no true contact of the soul with the object. Sensation does not experience any advancement to the rank of psychic feeling through its partial or absolute connection with representations.

Beforehand, a spiritual value, a life-force, must be noted in the appearance: beforehand, man must have wandered through the territory of experience, of education. He girds himself with all his demanding self-esteem and sets out to live and to act. An unquenchable urge for pleasure, for self-preservation, and self-reinforcement drives him about, and depending on the favorable or unfavorable success, his condition, his mood, is determined. Have these successes of utilitarian life, resonating in the state of the subject, in fact a human character? Who would want to deny that the farmer becomes sad at hail damage, and cheerful in fruitful weather? And yet, as long as this one farmer believes only himself to be affected, his feeling might have only a very relative degree of difference from sensation. Self-esteem, purely as such, is a dull, barren stirring which strives of itself out of itself and demands a corresponding counter-feeling. Man rises to a true life of feeling only in his fellow man. It is the love of nature for the species alone which enables me to have a complete spiritual transposition; with it, I feel not only myself, I feel at the same time also the feeling of another being.

A pure, complete connection of the subjective with the objective representation (intuition) can only come about when the latter in turn contains a human being. This applies equally to spiritual feeling, even if it were of the most egoistic nature; if only this egoism knows how to compare itself with the egoism of another. Sensation in league with the imagination only succeeds in the doubtful comparison with the external, peripheral, unspiritual aspects of the appearances. In feeling, however, a warmer gaze toward their spiritual core concentrates, without thereby surrendering the solidity of their bodily fullness. In the place of the thing, from which our body experiences a promotion or inhibition, there now steps a living individuality or a community of individuals which sympathetically feels and supports us, our life-situation, our life-urge, or which hinders us as something foreign and hateful. The scale of nerve and muscle movement, as it was applied above to the form of the impression in the case of sensation, applies here at the same time as a scale of meaningful life-movement in general. And the harmonic relationship between subject and object deepens here to one between subject and subject. Feeling thus rests on a promotion or disturbance of the whole human being as an individual life-force essentially related to its species.

It is the presentiment of the Good with which love enriches itself. Therefore, concepts like value, power, and significance no longer suffice for the characterization of the spiritual stimulus-content. They have now received an inner "world-valid"* luminosity, have become consecrated, festive bearers of a public dignity. The friendly person now appears to me generally as brave and noble; the hateful one, generally as reprobate and diabolical. I feel myself in myself or in another I, but only as a worthy representative of the whole species.

The progress is actually nothing other than a spiritual self-alienation and volatilization of the self-feeling, which henceforth only has itself in the whole. Thus, the compassion, the sympathy that we have, for example, with a wounded soldier, becomes a deep *Gemüth*-participation insofar as we expand the transposed, compassionate I to the general human-I, so that in this image of suffering, the purity of the entire human existence appears embittered with one stroke. The barbarism of hostility, the powerlessness of the individual, all this resigned collapsing, rattling down under the deluge of the tumult of life, as it is written on this face, it is repeated, and all of humanity must repeat it and experience it with him.

Mortality, however, can also be considered as a natural law that points us to our dependence at least as emphatically as the practical laws of human conflicts. —

When the farmer sees how the thunderstorm devastates his seed, how the avalanche smashes his house with wife and child, when he perceives all these negative oppositions which reach into his own life inevitably and more skillfully than the strongest of Cain's children, he may easily hit upon the thought that some human-like but superhuman beings are behind it. They disturb and fight him, though not everywhere and not always. They are therefore of different moods, or they divide themselves into two parties. Hence, he attempts to influence them through petitions and obedience to their presumed will, or also through threats. The primeval human being knows no real mechanical causes at all, but only causers or founders, and even today the charcoal burner curses his fire when it does not want to burn well. — One sees in the formation of myths the whole difficulty of naturally causal thinking. A change always has something very strange. One would hardly like to believe that the sun is suddenly on the left instead of on the right side. The naive human being helps himself simply with the example of his own changeable actions. He therefore assumes a personal conductor behind the things. Suada, the Goddess of persuasion, who, according to Sappho, was the offspring of Venus (Scholiast of Hesiod, *Works and Days*, 73), sprinkled it with perpetual gaiety. Encomiums to flowers occurred frequently there; to the rose in particular. "Sappho loves the rose, and always crowns it with some praise, likening the beautiful among virgins to it (Philostratus, *Letter* LXXIII)." In the Epithalamia, there was a sweetness of comparisons as fresh and flowery as the eternal beauties of nature from which the poetess borrowed them. There, as in the Catullan Epithalamium (*Vesper adest*; an imitation of the Sapphic, which is also embellished by Fragment LXV), two choirs were introduced, one of maidens, the other of young men; who gracefully contended, the former accusing, the latter defending, Hesperus. Fragment XLIII is a truly most delicate little painting, if it is truly ours. Let him study here who wants to know how to distinguish the Greek graces from the affectations of Arcadia. Fragment LIX, as Deschanel facetiously comments, brings us back to that of the Psalms (XXIV), on Palm Sunday: "Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of Glory shall enter."

IX.
By Tullius Laurea.
(III, 25, 64.)

Guest, you who pass by, grazing the Aeolian tomb, do not believe that the Muse of Mytilene is enclosed or extinguished within it. A mortal hand built this sepulcher; and every mortal work the rapid night of oblivion swallows. But if, for my sake, you wish to implore a favor from the Pierian Goddesses, who, one by one, enriched my nine books with a flower, you will know how I fled the shadows of Orcus <note>the underworld</note>; for the dawn shall never be dark for my lyre.

X.
By Antipater of Thessalonica.
(I, 67, 80.)
THE NINE GREEK POETESSES.

These women, tongues of heaven, Pierian women, were nourished by the hymns of Helicon and the Macedonian range: Praxilla and Myro and the speech of Anyte, the female Homer; and Sappho, whence the well-tressed virgins of Lesbos have luster;

But how do we arrive at this deep, dark, certain, intimate, and yet free feeling of oneness and togetherness? — "We may assume that every spiritual act occurs and is simultaneously reflected in certain vibrations—and who knows which ones?—of modifications of the nerve, in such a way that these represent its image; that, therefore, a symbolic imaging already takes place within the interior of the organism. The external phenomena, which affect us so peculiarly that we involuntarily attribute soul-moods to them, must relate to this inner imaging as its objective representation and decomposition; the assumed tendency of the nerve toward the relevant vibrations is met by the corresponding natural phenomenon, which awakens it to action, strengthens and confirms it, and therewith the movement of the soul reflected within it." "The different dimensions of line and surface, the differences in their movement, act symbolically; the vertical elevates, the horizontal expands, the curved moves more vividly than the straight, reminding one of the outward bending and inward turning of the inner life from and to given points and laws."

This is a theme before which many have already paused, but always only in passing. The first concentrated attempt to satisfy this question is made by J. V. Völker in his "Analysis and Symbolism" (1861).

Analysis and Symbolism (1861); a perceptive treatise to which I owe many encouragements and instructions for my own observation. However, the author, as clearly and sharply as the phenomena stand before him, does not quite arrive at a clear abstraction of the main concepts with which it is concerned, and around which all these impressions revolve. He himself confesses this in quite a candid manner (compare the preface). Incidentally, apart from personal reasons, it is always quite natural when such bold attempts, made almost without any premises of tradition or support from predecessors, have the character of a primitive, dark surging of thoughts. It is a somewhat murky, fermenting must, a young wine <note>original: "Sauser"</note> that the author pours for us. Unfortunately, he sometimes forgets, while pouring out foreign wines, to also stick their "labels" on the bottles.

The concept of "form-symbolism" was first clearly articulated and incorporated into the structure of systematic aesthetics by K. Köstlin (1862). And it is especially the concept of "associations of ideas" which is taken as the basis here (page 321).
